603.title: The dart of grief
603.hook: life is short and uncertain; draw out the dart of lamentation
603.howItsDone: Verses on impermanence are often chanted at Buddhist funerals and memorial services, and in many Theravada communities monks are invited to chant and teach for the family in the days after a death.

segments.voice: Yesterday: well spoken, four marks of good speech, and a poet who put them in verse. Your line: true and kind. Today, the hardest goodbye of all.

There's a drawer in many homes that nobody opens much. A watch that stopped. A card in a handwriting you'd know anywhere. A phone number you can't quite bring yourself to delete. Grief has a way of lodging somewhere and staying. The Salla Sutta, the discourse on the dart, eighth in the Sutta Nipata's third chapter, doesn't open with comfort. It opens with the plain facts of death, and then a picture every archer and every healer in ancient India would have known: something sharp, stuck in the chest, that has to come out.
screen: `A DRAWER NOBODY OPENS.` → `GRIEF LODGES AND STAYS.` → `THE SALLA SUTTA, SN 3.8.`

segments.voice: The verses begin bluntly. The life of mortals is unmarked by any sign of how long it will last, short, and tied up with pain. There's no way for those born not to die. Then the images pile up. As ripe fruit is in danger of falling early, so the born are always in danger of death. As clay pots made by a potter all end up broken, so it is with life. Young and old, foolish and wise, all go under death's power. Even as relatives look on, weeping, each one is led away. Then the turn. The wise, seeing how the world is, don't add grief on grief. Weeping and wailing, the poem says, don't bring back the one who's gone; they only harm the one who weeps, who grows thin and pale, while the dead are not helped at all. So draw out the dart: the dart of lamenting, of longing, of grief, and you'll find peace. Two things are worth noticing. First, the dart is in the mourner, not in the one who died. The poem isn't saying the loss doesn't matter. It's saying the wound is real and can heal. Second, Pali salla is a barbed arrow or a splinter, the thing a healer pulls out. The poem is firm: lamenting helps no one. But its picture is a healer's, not a judge's. A barb is drawn out with care, not something you're blamed for carrying.
screen: `NO SIGN OF HOW LONG.` · `RIPE FRUIT, CLAY POTS.` · `WEEPING DOESN'T BRING THEM BACK.` · `THE DART IS IN THE MOURNER.` · then, large: `DRAW OUT THE DART.`

segments.voice: If there's someone you've lost, a person, an animal, a time of your life, let them come to mind, and find where the feeling sits: the chest, the throat, behind the eyes. Breathe near it, the way you'd sit beside someone in a hospital bed. If nothing comes, think of someone who is grieving, and simply wish them ease.
Salla, a barbed dart. In the Salla Sutta, lamenting lodged in the one who mourns, a real wound, which can be drawn out.
Your line: draw out the dart. Gently, the way a healer would. Rest well, and see you tomorrow.

604.title: Only by deeds
604.hook: plants and animals differ by kind; humans differ only by what they do
604.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often cite the Vasettha Sutta when teaching that worth comes from conduct rather than birth.

segments.voice: Yesterday: salla, the dart of grief, a real wound in the mourner that can heal. Your line: draw out the dart. Today, two young men arrive mid-argument.

Two students, Vasettha and Bharadvaja, have been arguing on a walk. You may remember the name Vasettha from the Long Discourses. One says a person is a brahmin, a member of the priestly class, by birth: pure lineage on both sides, seven generations back. The other says no, by conduct. Neither can convince the other. So they do what friends still do when an argument stalls: they ask someone they both respect. The Buddha's answer, the ninth discourse of the Sutta Nipata's third chapter, starts not with people at all but with grass.
screen: `TWO STUDENTS, ONE ARGUMENT.` → `BY BIRTH OR BY CONDUCT?` → `ASK SOMEONE BOTH RESPECT.`

segments.voice: Look at grasses and trees, the Buddha says. They don't claim anything, yet their kinds are marked by birth; you can tell one from another. Worms, moths, ants. Four-footed animals, small and large. Snakes, fish, birds. Each kind has its own marks, given at birth. Among people, he says, there are no such marks of birth: not in the hair, the head, the ears, the eyes, the mouth, the nose, the lips, the neck, the hands, the feet. Bodies differ, of course; he isn't denying that. But nothing in the body marks out a separate kind. The differences people draw between each other are names they give. So what makes someone a farmer? Farming. A trader? Trading. A thief? Stealing. A priest? Performing the rites. And a true brahmin, in the noble sense the Buddha gives the word, is one who has let go, harms no one, is patient, honest, free. Then the line the whole answer leads to: the world goes on by action. Beings are bound to their deeds, the poem says, as a moving chariot is held by its linchpin. You heard a cousin of this a few weeks back, in the outcast discourse: not by birth, by deeds. Today adds the argument from nature. Grass is sorted by kind. People are known by what they do.

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you tend to file under a category: their accent, their job, their family, where they're from. Set the label down for a moment and ask only what this person does: maybe they're patient with a child, maybe they show up early. Let the label go quiet, and let one deed stand there instead.
Kamma, deed or action. In the Vasettha Sutta, people aren't sorted by birth the way plants and animals are; they're known by what they do.
Your line: held by its linchpin. The wheel turns on what is done. That's day six hundred four.

605.title: The axe in the mouth
605.hook: a person is born with an axe in the mouth and cuts himself with bad speech
605.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often quote the axe-in-the-mouth verse when teaching right speech, and lay Buddhists who keep the five precepts include one against false speech.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kamma, people known by what they do, not by birth. Your line: held by its linchpin. Today, a deed done with the tongue.

Three days ago you heard the four marks of good speech. Today the Sutta Nipata shows the other side, with a story. A monk named Kokaliya comes to the Buddha with a complaint about two other monks. Not just any two: Sariputta and Moggallana, the Buddha's two chief disciples. They have bad intentions, Kokaliya says. The Buddha answers him three times with the same words. What happens next is hard to hear.
screen: `A COMPLAINT ABOUT TWO MONKS.` → `THE TWO CHIEF DISCIPLES.` → `THE SAME ANSWER, THREE TIMES.`

segments.voice: Don't say that, Kokaliya, the Buddha tells him. Have confidence in Sariputta and Moggallana; they are good. Kokaliya repeats the charge. The Buddha repeats the answer. A third time, the same. Kokaliya gets up and leaves. Then, the text says, his body breaks out in boils, small as mustard seeds at first, growing larger and larger until they burst, and he dies. The text says he is reborn in the hell called Paduma, and describes its torments at length, in the vivid, frightening terms the early texts use for the results of harmful acts. The lesson is in the verses. A person is born, they say, with an axe in the mouth, and the fool cuts himself with it when he speaks badly. Look where the blade lands. Not on Sariputta and Moggallana. On Kokaliya. Whoever praises someone who deserves blame, or blames someone who deserves praise, gathers bad luck with his own mouth. A loss at dice, the verses say, is small next to this. And notice what the Buddha did. He didn't argue. He didn't punish. He said the true thing, kindly, three times, and left the choice with Kokaliya.

Bring to mind one person you're tempted to complain about, notice the sentence that's ready to go, and see who it would cut first. Then let it rest, unspoken, and come back to the breath at the lips.
Kuthari, an axe. In the Kokaliya Sutta, the image for harmful speech: a blade a person is born with, which cuts the speaker first.
Your line: let one word stay home. Some words do the most good unsaid. Day six hundred five.

606.title: Deep rivers are quiet
606.hook: to Nalaka: shallow streams are noisy, the great river flows quietly
606.howItsDone: Many Buddhist monasteries keep times of noble silence, and lay retreats often run for days with little or no talking, as a way of letting the mind settle.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kuthari, the axe in the mouth that cuts the speaker first. Your line: let one word stay home. Today, the opposite of a busy tongue.

Early on this path, you met an old sage named Asita. He held the newborn prince, smiled, and then wept, because he knew he wouldn't live long enough to hear this child teach. The Sutta Nipata keeps that scene as the opening of a longer poem, and adds something you didn't hear then. Before he died, Asita told his nephew, a young man named Nalaka: when you hear that this one has awakened, go to him. Nalaka waited. Years later, he went.
screen: `ASITA WEEPS OVER THE CHILD.` → `HE TELLS HIS NEPHEW: GO TO HIM.` → `YEARS LATER, NALAKA GOES.`

segments.voice: Nalaka asks about the life of a sage, what the Pali calls moneyya, the way of silence. The Buddha warns him first that it's hard, then gives a long answer: be the same whether praised or insulted; go for alms without lingering, without wanting more; don't make a show of yourself. Toward the end comes the image. Learn it, he says, from the water. In the clefts and gullies, the little streams run noisily. The great waters move in silence. Then plainly: what is lacking makes a noise; what is full is quiet. And one more picture: the fool is like a half-full pot, sloshing; the wise one is like a lake filled to the brim. A half-full water jug in the back of a car slaps and gurgles at every bump. A full one makes no sound at all. The poem isn't saying never speak. The same answer praises a sage who speaks, when he does, about what is useful and true. When the sage teaches, he teaches from what he knows, without excess. The noise comes from the gap, from the part that's empty and wants to be seen. So the quiet isn't a rule of silence. It's what fullness sounds like.

segments.voice: Picture a wide, slow river at evening: so much moving under the surface, and so little sound. Notice your own inner chatter, the little streams, without trying to stop it. Let the breath go deeper and slower beneath it, like the river under the ripples, and rest down there.
Moneyya, the way of silence. The Buddha's image for Nalaka: little streams rush noisily, the great waters move in silence; what's empty makes noise, what's full is still.
Your line: what is full is quiet. A pause doesn't always need filling. Until tomorrow.

607.title: The chapter of eights
607.hook: sixteen short poems against clinging to views
607.howItsDone: The Atthakavagga is studied in Theravada monasteries and widely read by lay Buddhists and scholars for its early style; teachers often draw on it when speaking about letting go of attachment to views.

segments.voice: Yesterday: moneyya, the sage's way of silence, learned from the water. Your line: what is full is quiet. Today, the Sutta Nipata's fourth chapter.

An argument online: two people, each certain, each quoting, each getting louder. Neither one changes the other's mind, and both log off a little more sure they were right. A set of old poems looks at that exact scene and asks a strange question. Not who's right. What happens to a person who needs to be? That's the fourth chapter of the Sutta Nipata: sixteen short poems with a curious name, the Atthakavagga, the chapter of eights.
screen: `TWO PEOPLE, EACH CERTAIN.` → `NOT WHO'S RIGHT.` → `WHAT HAPPENS TO THE ONE WHO NEEDS TO BE?`

segments.voice: Atthaka means a group of eight, and vagga means a chapter. The name probably comes from several of its poems that have eight verses each: the eights on the cave, on the corrupted, on the pure, on the supreme. Not all sixteen do. Some scholars count this chapter among the early layers of Buddhist verse, partly because other parts of the canon know it by name. In the Udana, a monk named Sona is invited to recite, and he chants all sixteen poems of the eights from memory; the Buddha praises how well he has learned them. In that story, the poems are already a set, known by heart. And what do they say? Again and again, the same thing from different sides. People hold a view and call it the best. They call everyone else's foolish. They go into the assembly to argue, hungry for praise, and if they lose, they're stung. The sage, the poems say, doesn't step into that ring. Not because he has a cleverer view, but because he doesn't grasp any view as the thing that makes him pure. Some lines are hard, and teachers read them in different ways: does the sage hold no views at all, or hold them lightly? The poems themselves leave room for both.
screen: `ATTHAKA: A GROUP OF EIGHT.` · `KNOWN BY NAME ELSEWHERE.` · `SONA CHANTS THEM FROM MEMORY.` · `THE SAGE DOESN'T ENTER THE RING.` · then, large: `NO VIEW TO CLING TO.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one opinion you hold strongly, not to drop it, only to notice how it sits in the body when you think of someone who disagrees: the jaw, the chest, the hands. Notice the wanting to win. Then let the breath soften that place, and let the opinion simply be an opinion, held in an open hand.
Atthakavagga. The chapter of eights, the fourth chapter of the Sutta Nipata: sixteen short, old poems on not clinging to views.
Your line: no view to cling to. Being right and being free aren't always the same thing. That's day six hundred seven.

608.title: Fear from the rod
608.hook: fear is born from taking up the rod; see the fish in shrinking water
608.tomorrow: The way to the far shore
608.howItsDone: Teachers in several Buddhist traditions read the Attadanda Sutta as an account of the urgency, or samvega, that turns a person toward practice, and it is often cited in teaching on nonviolence.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Atthakavagga, the chapter of eights, and the sage who stays out of the ring. Your line: no view to cling to. Today, that chapter's last poem.

A pond at the end of a long dry season. The water has shrunk to a muddy patch in the middle, and the fish are crowded into it, flapping, pushing against each other for the last of it. That image is at the heart of the Atthakavagga's final poem, Sutta Nipata 4.15. And unlike most discourses, it's spoken in the first person. The speaker tells what he saw, and how it shook him, before he ever found peace.
screen: `A POND AT THE END OF THE DRY SEASON.` → `FISH CROWDED IN THE MUD.` → `SPOKEN IN THE FIRST PERSON.`

segments.voice: The poem opens with a line that could stand alone: fear is born from the one who takes up the rod. Atta danda: the rod taken up, the stick picked up to strike. Look at people quarreling, the speaker says. Then his own alarm. I saw people trembling, like fish in little water, set against one another, and fear came into me. The world seemed to have no core; every direction was shaken. I looked for a place for myself and found none that wasn't already claimed. Seeing everyone in conflict to the end, I was disturbed. Then the turn. I saw a dart, he says, hard to see, lodged in the heart. Pulled along by that dart, people run in every direction. Pull it out, and you don't run, and you don't sink. Two things are worth holding. First, the line about the rod cuts both ways: the one who picks up the stick creates fear in others, and also lives in fear. Second, the cause isn't finally the other fish. It's the dart inside, the craving and grasping, that makes the pond feel so small. Commentaries set the poem during a quarrel between two clans, the Sakyans and the Koliyans, over the water of a river. The poem itself names no one.
screen: `THE ONE WHO TAKES UP THE ROD.` · `FISH IN LITTLE WATER.` · `NO PLACE NOT ALREADY CLAIMED.` · `A DART HARD TO SEE.` · then, large: `FEAR BORN FROM THE ROD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a conflict you're part of, large or small: a sibling, a neighbor, a group chat, and ask what patch of water you're both fighting for: being right, being respected, being safe? Look for the dart in your own chest, the wanting that keeps you flapping, without pulling hard. Just see it, and let the breath settle around it.
Attadanda, the rod taken up. The opening of Sutta Nipata 4.15: whoever takes up the stick to strike breeds fear, in others and in themselves.
Your line: fear born from the rod. The one who sets the stick down has less to fear. Day six hundred eight, done.

chat.says: That poem about fish in a shrinking pond: what does it say causes fear?
options: Taking up the rod breeds fear both ways, and the root is a dart inside.
The other fish; if they'd leave, the pond would feel big enough.
The dry season; fear comes only from outside events like drought.
chat.meaning: Fear is born from taking up the rod, in others and in yourself. The poem finds the cause in a dart lodged in the heart: craving and grasping.

609.title: The way to the far shore
609.hook: sixteen young brahmins bring their questions, and each is answered
609.howItsDone: The Parayanavagga is studied in Theravada monasteries and often taught one question at a time; its image of crossing the flood to the far shore runs through Buddhist chanting and teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday: attadanda, the rod taken up, and fish in a shrinking pond. Your line: fear born from the rod. Today closes a week and opens the Sutta Nipata's last chapter.

Far to the south, on the banks of the Godavari river, an old brahmin teacher named Bavari is living quietly when a visitor arrives, demands money, and, when Bavari has none to give, curses him: in seven days your head will split in seven pieces. Bavari is shaken. A kindly spirit tells him that the visitor knows nothing about heads splitting, but that someone in the north does know: a Buddha. Bavari doesn't go himself. He sends his sixteen students instead.
screen: `AN OLD TEACHER BY THE GODAVARI.` → `A CURSE, AND A FRIGHT.` → `SIXTEEN STUDENTS SENT NORTH.`

segments.voice: The prologue to the Sutta Nipata's fifth chapter traces their road north town by town, until they find the Buddha at a rocky shrine near Rajagaha. They ask Bavari's questions first, about the head and its splitting, and the Buddha answers that ignorance is the head, and knowledge, with faith, mindfulness and effort, is what splits it. Then each of the sixteen asks his own. Ajita asks what the world is wrapped in. Mettagu asks where suffering comes from. Upasiva asks what to lean on to cross. Hemaka, Todeyya, Kappa, Mogharaja: each brings something real, and each gets an answer shaped to him. That's the striking thing about this chapter. It isn't one teaching to a crowd. It's sixteen conversations. The word that names it, parayana, means the way to the beyond, the going to the far shore. And the image running through it is a flood: the rushing water of craving and views that has to be crossed. At the end, Pingiya, old and frail by his own account, goes home and sings the Buddha's praise to Bavari. The week behind: the dart of grief, only by deeds, the axe in the mouth, deep rivers are quiet, no view to cling to, fear from the rod. Now sixteen questions, and a river to cross.
screen: `A LONG ROAD NORTH.` · `IGNORANCE IS THE HEAD.` · `SIXTEEN QUESTIONS, SIXTEEN ANSWERS.` · `THE FLOOD TO BE CROSSED.` · then, large: `CROSSING THE FLOOD.`

segments.voice: If you had walked that far to ask one question, what would it be? Not a clever one, but the one that's actually there, under the others. Let it come slowly, and when it does, don't answer it; just hold it, the way the students held theirs on the road.
Parayana. The way to the far shore, the last chapter of the Sutta Nipata, where sixteen students each ask their question.
Your line: crossing the flood. A real question is worth the walk. Another week, complete.

chat.says: Why is that last chapter called the way to the far shore?
options: Its sixteen talks are about crossing the flood of craving and views.
It records the Buddha's boat trip south to visit Bavari's home.
It just maps the students' road north, town by town, to Rajagaha.
chat.meaning: Parayana means the way to the beyond. Through sixteen conversations, its image is a flood of craving and views that has to be crossed.
